I have something I call the 'three breath rule'. When I am talking to someone, if I draw three breaths, I need to wrap up what I'm saying so I'm not 'talking at' them. If you do that, people switch off; it's too much information, it's a lecture, they want it to be over and they're losing focus.

You often need to get ideas across in stages; nothing sinks in all at once. You can't just tell someone what you see as the truth when it's different to what they see as the truth, and have them just go with you on that. Our brains do not like being forced to rewire too much at once - we're like a donkey in a lighthouse, we don't want to go backwards. So bit by bit. If he makes a point, don't shoot it straight down - ask what he thinks about aspects he might not have thought of, and tell him what you think - just as 'this is my take on it' rather than 'this is what's happening!'

In order to change someone's mind, you have to work on gently and kind of almost consentually dismantle preconceptions without destroying good ideas within them.

It's super helpful to start from a point of finding out what you agree on. This is good in any argument - it's easier to argue out from a common pool of agreed-upon 'facts' than to pick out stuff you disagree with and try to win point by point.

This is good for you as well as them, because they may have points that you haven't figured in yet, they may see certain things with more understanding than you because of their experience or knowledge, and if you make this a journey and a learning discussion in which you converse about it rather than trying to convince each other, you will end up with the sum of both your analysis, and you'll encourage a spirit of cooperation in which your ideas are considered and listened to because you present them in a reasonable and well-thought out way that invites discussion.
